sections.title: Fine-tuning methods matched to your task, data and budget
sections.description: We recommend the lightest method that meets your quality target — and tell you when prompting or RAG will do the job instead.

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA / QLoRA)
items.description: Adapt 7B–70B open-weight models such as Llama 3 and Mistral by training only a small fraction of parameters — lower GPU cost, faster iteration and deployable on modest hardware.
items.label: Most Common

items.title: Full Fine-Tuning
items.description: Update all model weights when a task needs deeper adaptation than LoRA can deliver — for small models on focused datasets or large models at enterprise scale.
items.label: Deep Adaptation

items.title: Instruction Fine-Tuning
items.description: Train a custom chat or task model to follow your instructions, output formats and tone consistently — useful when prompting alone produces inconsistent structure.
items.label: Custom Chat Models

items.title: API Model Fine-Tuning
items.description: Fine-tune hosted models such as GPT-4o through the provider's fine-tuning API when you want managed serving and accept provider-side data handling.
items.label: Managed

items.title: Embedding Model Fine-Tuning
items.description: Improve retrieval quality for RAG and semantic search by adapting embedding models to your domain's vocabulary and relevance judgments.
items.label: For RAG

items.title: Classifier Fine-Tuning and Domain Pre-Training
items.description: Fine-tune BERT/RoBERTa-class models for high-volume classification, or continue pre-training on domain corpora when vocabulary differs sharply from general text.
items.label: Specialized

sections.title: When fine-tuning is the right tool — and when it isn't

blocks.heading: Fine-tuning is better when
paragraphs: You need a consistent style, tone or persona, a specific output format that prompting does not reliably produce, or task-specific behaviour learned from many high-quality examples.

blocks.heading: RAG is better when
paragraphs: Your knowledge changes frequently, answers must cite sources, or you work across large and varied document collections. Fine-tuning improves format and style more reliably than it improves factual accuracy.

blocks.heading: Both together
paragraphs: For the highest performance, fine-tune the model for style, format and task behaviour while RAG supplies the knowledge to retrieve from.

items.question: How much does AI model fine-tuning cost?
items.answer: $5,000–$120,000 depending on model size and method. LoRA fine-tuning on 7B–13B models: $8,000–$35,000. Full fine-tuning on large models: $40,000–$120,000. Training data collection usually represents the largest cost component.

items.question: Do we need fine-tuning or will prompt engineering and RAG work?
items.answer: Try prompt engineering and RAG first — they're cheaper and faster. Fine-tuning adds the most value when the model needs to learn a specific style or output format that prompting doesn't reliably produce.

items.question: How long does fine-tuning take?
items.answer: 3–20 weeks depending on dataset preparation and model size. Dataset preparation is typically the longest phase.

items.question: How many training examples does fine-tuning require?
items.answer: Depends on the task. Classification: 500–2,000 per class. Instruction following: 1,000–10,000. Domain adaptation: 500–5,000.

items.question: Can fine-tuning work with proprietary data that can't leave our servers?
items.answer: Yes — self-hosted LoRA fine-tuning on Llama 3 or Mistral keeps all training data within your infrastructure, on your cloud account or on-premises GPU servers.

items.question: Who owns the fine-tuned model weights?
items.answer: You do — ClickMasters transfers model weights, training code, evaluation scripts and dataset preparation pipelines at project close.
